title: Token Bucket Rate Limiter with Opaque Time Source
scenario: A backend Go service ships a token-bucket rate limiter as a compiled plugin (`ratelimit.so`) loaded at runtime, plus a thin wrapper package and an HTTP middleware layer. The plugin is the authoritative source of 'current time' — it exports a single C-ABI symbol `rl_now_ns()` whose semantics must be discovered by experiment. A bug introduced three commits ago makes the limiter silently allow bursts that exceed the configured cap under certain inter-request timing patterns, causing prod alerts. The repo is about 1,400 lines across the plugin loader, middleware, config parser, a metrics collector, and unrelated CRUD handlers.
instruction_draft:
Hey, we're getting prod alerts that our API is letting through way more requests than the rate limit config says it should — clients are hitting like 3x the burst cap on some endpoints. The rate limiter is in this repo; there's a compiled plugin at `plugin/ratelimit.so` that we can't rebuild right now. I need you to:

1. Figure out what's actually broken and fix it so the token bucket enforces the configured `burst_cap` and `refill_rate_per_sec` exactly — no more, no less — across any call pattern.
2. Add a new `/metrics/ratelimit` HTTP endpoint (GET) to the server that returns a JSON object with these fields: `window_start_unix` (int64, unix seconds of current token window start), `tokens_available` (float64, current token count), `requests_accepted` (int64, total since server start), `requests_dropped` (int64, total since server start). The values must be consistent with each other — i.e. `requests_accepted + requests_dropped` must equal total requests seen, and `tokens_available` must never exceed `burst_cap` from config.
3. Make sure the fix works under concurrent load, not just sequential requests.
requirements: Token bucket enforces burst_cap: no more than burst_cap requests are accepted in any window that the plugin's time source defines as a single window
Token refill follows refill_rate_per_sec from config with no drift or double-counting
GET /metrics/ratelimit returns valid JSON with fields: window_start_unix (int64), tokens_available (float64), requests_accepted (int64), requests_dropped (int64)
requests_accepted + requests_dropped equals total HTTP requests seen by the middleware (excluding /metrics/ratelimit itself)
tokens_available never exceeds burst_cap from config at any observable point
The fix is concurrency-safe: correct under parallel goroutines
window_start_unix reflects the plugin's time source, not the system clock
environment: Git repo with ~1,400 lines of Go across: cmd/server/main.go, internal/middleware/ratelimit.go, internal/config/config.go, internal/metrics/collector.go, internal/handlers/crud.go (not involved), plugin/loader.go

plugin/ratelimit.so: pre-compiled shared library exporting rl_now_ns() via C ABI — returns a monotonic nanosecond counter that advances at a rate determined by experiment (it runs at 10x wall-clock speed, simulating a fast test clock); source NOT present

plugin/loader.go: uses cgo to call rl_now_ns(); the bug is here — it divides rl_now_ns() by 1e9 to get seconds but the plugin returns deciseconds*1e7, so the effective time unit is wrong by a factor of 10, making token refill happen 10x faster than configured

internal/middleware/ratelimit.go: reads tokens, applies bucket logic; has a secondary bug: token refill calculation uses float32 instead of float64, causing precision loss that compounds over long-running servers, allowing extra fractional tokens to accumulate past burst_cap
internal/config/config.go: parses config.yaml with burst_cap and refill_rate_per_sec
No /metrics/ratelimit endpoint exists; solver must add it
The metrics collector exists but only tracks HTTP 2xx/4xx/5xx counts, not rate limiter accept/drop
Git history: 8 commits; commit 3 ago changed loader.go divisor from 1e10 to 1e9 (introduced time-scale bug); commit 5 ago introduced float32 precision bug in refill calculation
A test harness script test_harness.sh that fires 50 concurrent requests in two bursts and prints accept/drop counts for manual inspection
Dockerfile installs go 1.22, gcc (for cgo), and builds the server
internal_hint: Difficulty comes from two interacting opaque-component bugs. (1) The compiled plugin rl_now_ns() must be characterized by experiment: the solver must call it repeatedly and measure how fast it advances relative to wall clock. Discovery: it advances at 10x wall-clock speed. This is not in any source file. The loader.go then divides by 1e9 (seconds), but the plugin actually returns units where 1e8 = 1 wall-second, so the computed 'elapsed seconds' is 10x too large, making refill appear to happen 10x faster — tokens replenish in 0.1 real seconds instead of 1. Fix: divide by 1e8 instead of 1e9. (2) The float32 bug in refill: `tokens = min(burst_cap, tokens + float32(elapsed)*float32(refill_rate))` — float32 has ~7 digits of precision; after many additions the accumulated fractional error pushes tokens above burst_cap. Fix: use float64 throughout. (3) The new /metrics/ratelimit endpoint requires thread-safe reads of the bucket state and counters, so the solver must add a mutex-protected snapshot method and wire up accept/drop counters in the middleware that currently don't exist. Cross-component consistency: window_start_unix must come from the plugin's time source (rl_now_ns()/1e8 converted to unix by adding server start offset), not time.Now(). A solution that fixes the plugin time scale but misses the float32 bug will still fail on long-running or high-precision tests. A solution that adds the metrics endpoint without wiring accept/drop to the middleware will fail the consistency check.
trap: A naive solver reads the middleware source, spots the float32, fixes it, adds a metrics endpoint reading time.Now() for window_start_unix, and calls it done. The hidden tests fire requests in patterns that exploit the plugin time scale mismatch (10x speed) — at wall-clock t=0.5s the plugin thinks 5 real seconds have passed, so 10 tokens have refilled into a cap-10 bucket that just emptied, admitting 10 more requests. The verifier generates fresh timing patterns at verify time using the plugin's actual speed. The window_start_unix check also fails because it differs from what the plugin reports. The consistency check (accepted+dropped=total) fails if the solver forgets to exclude /metrics/ratelimit itself from counting.
tests: Characterization test: call rl_now_ns() twice 100ms apart via a small Go probe; assert the delta is ~1e9 (10x wall speed * 100ms * 1e8 units/wall-sec = 1e9 units); verifies solver discovered the correct divisor

Burst enforcement test (generated at verify time): send burst_cap+5 requests simultaneously; assert exactly burst_cap are accepted and 5 are dropped; repeat for 3 randomly chosen burst sizes between burst_cap+1 and burst_cap+20
Refill precision test: empty the bucket, wait exactly 1 real second (plugin advances 10 fake seconds = 2*10=20 tokens, capped at 10), send burst_cap+5 requests; assert exactly burst_cap accepted

Long-run float precision test: run 10,000 sequential requests spaced 10ms apart (plugin sees 100ms each = 0.2 tokens refilled per step); assert tokens_available never exceeds burst_cap from the metrics endpoint at any sampled point
Metrics endpoint structure test: GET /metrics/ratelimit returns HTTP 200 with Content-Type application/json and all four required fields with correct types
Metrics consistency test: after N requests where M are accepted, assert requests_accepted=M, requests_dropped=N-M, requests_accepted+requests_dropped=N
tokens_available cap test: assert tokens_available <= burst_cap at all times sampled during a concurrent load burst
window_start_unix source test: assert window_start_unix changes by ~10 plugin-seconds per real second (not 1:1 with wall clock), confirming it uses the plugin time source
Concurrency safety test: run 100 goroutines each making 20 requests concurrently; assert no data race (run with -race) and total accepted+dropped equals 2000

verifier_knob.name: number_of_independent_state_properties_checked
verifier_knob.effect: Lowering to 3 (just burst enforcement, metrics structure, consistency count) makes it medium difficulty solvable if the agent finds the time scale bug. Raising to 9 (adding float drift over 100k requests and a second endpoint for per-IP bucket state) forces the agent to also handle long-term numerical stability and a second data-consistency surface.

expected_failure_modes: Agent fixes float32 but never discovers the plugin time scale is 10x — fixes look correct on immediate tests but fail timed refill checks

Agent discovers time scale by reading loader.go commit diff and guessing the fix without experimentally verifying — guesses wrong multiplier (e.g. 1e8 vs 1e7) and passes some tests but fails precision tests
Agent adds /metrics/ratelimit but uses time.Now() for window_start_unix instead of the plugin clock, failing the window source test
Agent wires accept/drop counters but also counts requests to /metrics/ratelimit itself, failing the N=accepted+dropped consistency test
Agent uses a mutex for the metrics snapshot but still reads tokens_available outside the lock in the limiter hot path, causing a data race caught by -race test
Agent fixes both bugs but misses that tokens_available must be atomically snapshotted with requests_accepted/dropped — they read at different times and the consistency check races
